sweep:foundation-models.angle: PRETRAINED PPG ENCODERS: open-weight foundation / self-supervised models for PPG and wearable biosignals, their input formats, licenses, sizes, evidence of transfer to regression (incl. glucose), and feasibility as frozen feature extractors + ridge/MLP probe on an M4 MacBook Air 16 GB (PyTorch/MPS).

findings.title: PaPaGei-S / PaPaGei-P (Nokia Bell Labs, ICLR 2025) -- OPEN WEIGHTS, best-documented, smallest
findings.summary: Weights: Zenodo 13983110, files papagei_s.pt (23.3 MB), papagei_p.pt (20.2 MB), papagei_s_svri.pt (20.1 MB); Zenodo record states no explicit license for the weights (only lists source-data licenses VitalDB CC-BY-4.0, MIMIC-III ODbL); code is BSD-3. Size: ~5.7M params (PaPaGei-S; expert heads dropped at inference), PaPaGei-P ~5M. Backbone: 1D ResNet, 18 conv blocks, base 32 filters doubling every 4 blocks, kernel 3, stride 2, linear projection to 512-d embedding (class ResNet1DMoE(in_channels=1, base_filters=32, kernel_size=3, stride=2, groups=1, n_block=18, n_classes=512, n_experts=3); model(x)[0] gives embeddings). Input: single channel, 125 Hz, 10-s non-overlapping segments (1250 samples), 4th-order Chebyshev band-pass 0.5-12 Hz, z-score; segments with >25% flatline removed; tensor (N,1,1250); README shows resample_batch_signal(fs_original -> 125). Pretraining: VitalDB + MIMIC-III waveform + MESA, 13,517 participants, ~20.75M segments, ~57,641 h, 8xV100, 15k steps. Evaluation protocol: frozen encoder, linear probe (ridge for regression, logistic for binary, RF for multiclass), subject-level splits, 500-bootstrap CIs. Regression results (MAE, PaPaGei-S vs best of Chronos/MOMENT/REGLE): SBP PPG-BP 14.39 vs 14.50; DBP PPG-BP 8.71 vs 9.30; avg HR PPG-BP 4.00 vs 4.41; SBP VitalVideos 14.65 vs 14.71; DBP 8.29 vs 8.65; AHI 12.97 vs 14.06; HR DaLiA 11.53 vs 8.82 (MOMENT better); gestational age 6.05 vs 5.69 (Chronos better). Average regression MAE 10.12 (PaPaGei-S) vs MOMENT 10.43, Chronos 11.60, REGLE 12.09. Glucose/diabetes/HbA1c: NOT evaluated. Third-party VitalDB age benchmark (https://github.com/Misterbra/ppg-age-benchmark, 906 subjects, 5-fold, linear probe): PaPaGei-S MAE 9.80±0.34 y, R2 0.313 vs predict-mean 11.91 y.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Most practical first candidate. Mendeley recordings are exactly 10 s, so each recording resampled 2175 -> 125 Hz is one native PaPaGei segment (1250 samples) with no windowing; BIG IDEAs 10 s before each CGM reading (E4 64 Hz -> 125 Hz) also fits. 23 MB / 5.7M params: trivially runs on MPS or even CPU; embedding all Mendeley recordings takes seconds. Note mismatch with our 0.5-8 Hz / 64 Hz / 5-s pipeline: must re-derive 125 Hz, 0.5-12 Hz, 10-s inputs from raw. Weights license is unstated on Zenodo (code BSD-3) -- fine for a research evaluation, but state it.

findings.title: Pulse-PPG (UIUC/Memphis, IMWUT 2025) -- OPEN WEIGHTS, field/wearable-trained, MIT
findings.source: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01108 (Proc. ACM IMWUT 9(3) 2025, https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3749494). Code: https://github.com/maxxu05/pulseppg (MIT). Weights: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17270930 (concept DOI; version record https://zenodo.org/records/17345536, pulseppg_model_weights.zip 315.3 MB, MIT)
findings.summary: Weights: Zenodo (MIT license on the record), 315.3 MB zip, fetched by download script in repo (README says ./download_pulseppg.sh; file listing shows download_model.sh). Size: 1D ResNet-26, 28.5M trainable params (initial filters 128, kernel 11, stride 2, 12 residual blocks), 512-d embedding; global average pooling so variable-length input. Input: field PPG from a 100-day, 120-participant study (MOODS; paper is inconsistent on 100 vs 50 Hz raw), all downstream signals resampled to 50 Hz; NO band-pass filtering; global person-specific z-score plus instance-norm at the first layer; pretrained on 4-min windows (12,000 samples at 50 Hz) but README says other lengths (e.g. 30 s) work. Evaluation: linear probe on frozen 512-d embeddings (L2 logistic / L2 linear regression, StandardScaler, CV grid search), subject-wise splits; fine-tuning also reported. Regression tasks: instant HR (PPG-DaLiA), SBP/DBP/avg HR (PPG-BP). Reported: beats PaPaGei-S on 10/11 tasks; instant HR MAE improved by 6.28 bpm; clinical regression MAE improved by ~0.5; average MAPE 0.1009 vs PaPaGei 0.1288. Glucose/diabetes/HbA1c: NOT evaluated (glucose only in intro). Third-party VitalDB age probe: MAE 9.28±0.44 y, R2 0.388 (best of the open models); +demographics 8.22 y. README notes configs currently support linear probing only.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Closest to our BIG IDEAs setting: trained on wrist-worn, uncurated field PPG, so the domain gap to Empatica E4 BVP is smallest. Our loader already caches 2 min of BVP around every CGM reading, so a 60-s pre-reading window at 50 Hz (64 -> 50 Hz) is available without re-downloading; for Mendeley only 10 s exists (500 samples at 50 Hz), far shorter than the 4-min pretraining windows -- report as a caveat. 28.5M params / ~115 MB fp32 runs comfortably on MPS. MIT license is the cleanest of all candidates.

findings.title: AnyPPG (PKU Digital Health, KDD 2026) -- OPEN WEIGHTS, ECG-guided, 16 MB checkpoint, no license file
findings.source: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01747 (html: https://arxiv.org/html/2511.01747). Code+weights: https://github.com/PKUDigitalHealth/AnyPPG (checkpoint load_anyppg/anyppg_ckpt.pth, 16,375,441 bytes per GitHub API; repo license field null; description '[KDD 2026] A PPG Foundation Model for Comprehensive Assessment of Multi-organ Health')
findings.summary: Weights: in-repo file anyppg_ckpt.pth, ~16.4 MB (so roughly 4M fp32 params). Backbone: Net1D (ResNet-derived 1D CNN; cfg in_channels=1, base_filters=64, filter_list=[64,160,160,400,400,512], m_blocks_list=[2,2,2,3,3,1], kernel 3, stride 2, groups_width 16), 512-d output; demo: x=torch.randn(1,1,1250) -> (1,512). Input: 125 Hz, 10-s non-overlapping segments, PPG band-pass 0.5-8 Hz, z-score along time; no PPG quality filtering. Pretraining: contrastive alignment to a frozen ECG encoder (ECGFounder) on ~40M paired 10-s PPG-ECG segments: MC-MED 49,916 subj / 78,945 h, PulseDB 4,964 / 12,768 h, MESA 2,010 / 7,947 h, HSP 1,584 / 9,260 h, CFS 322 / 989 h; total 58,796 subjects, 109,909 h. Evaluation: linear probe (ridge for regression, inner 5-fold CV); 15 tasks on 8 datasets; best on 13/15, beats PaPaGei-S/P and Pulse-PPG on 14/15. Regression MAEs (linear probe): DaLiA HR 9.27; BUT PPG HR 5.47; UCI-BP SBP 15.62 / DBP 7.14; WenXinWuYang HR 6.83, RR 2.30, age 6.08. Phenome-wide fine-tune on MC-MED: AUC>=0.70 for 307 of 1,468 phecodes. Glucose/HbA1c: not a downstream task; diabetes only in related work (phecode study may include diabetes codes but no number extracted). License: none in repo (GitHub license=null).
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Second cheap candidate: same 125 Hz / 10 s format as PaPaGei and the same 0.5-8 Hz band-pass we already use, so one preprocessing path serves both. 16 MB checkpoint, MPS-trivial. No license file: usable for a research evaluation but we cannot redistribute embeddings/weights; cite the repo. Load with torch.load(..., map_location='cpu', weights_only=True).

findings.title: SIGMA-PPG (2026) -- OPEN WEIGHTS on Hugging Face (363 MB), generative masked model, no license
findings.source: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21031. Code: https://github.com/ZonghengGuo/SigmaPPG (license null). Weights: https://huggingface.co/zonhengu/sigmappg/tree/main (sigma.pth, 363 MB, pickle; no model card/license)
findings.summary: Statistical-prior informed generative masking architecture with prior-guided adversarial masking and a VQ tokenizer (vqnsp_encoder_base_decoder_3x250x12, codebook 4096 x 64). Pretrained on >120,000 h of PPG. Input: 50 Hz, patch size 50 (1 s), quick-start input_size 1000 samples (20 s), pretraining input_size 12000 (240 s); shape [B,C,L] rearranged to patches; preprocessing via preprocessing_main.py (MIMIC-III example), no filter details on page. Loading: downstream.model_select.select_model(backbone='sigma_ppg_pro', pretrained=True, checkpoint_path='sigma.pth', freeze_backbone_flag=..., patch_size=50, input_size=1000). Parameter count not stated (363 MB checkpoint incl. tokenizer -> order 10^8 params). 12 downstream tasks vs 5 baselines (only HR on BIDMC named in README). Glucose: not evaluated. In PPG-LM's frozen-probe comparison it scored R2 0.028-0.041 on MC-MED glucose (see PPG-LM entry).
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Feasible on MPS (a few hundred MB), but least documented: no license, pickled checkpoint (7 detected pickle imports incl. argparse.Namespace, so weights_only=True may fail), custom patch pipeline. Third priority; include only if the first three run cleanly.

findings.title: NormWear (UCSD, ACM TCH 2026) -- OPEN WEIGHTS, multimodal scalogram transformer, Apache-2.0, 0.2B params
findings.source: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09758 (html: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2412.09758). Code: https://github.com/Mobile-Sensing-and-UbiComp-Laboratory/NormWear (Apache-2.0; checkpoint in GitHub release v1.0.0-alpha). HF: https://huggingface.co/mosaic-laboratory/normwear (apache-2.0, 0.2B params F32, AutoModel.from_pretrained(..., trust_remote_code=True))
findings.summary: Architecture: conv patching + 12-block transformer encoder with 6 interleaved channel-fusion blocks (18 blocks, hidden 768, 12 heads, FF 3072), per-channel [CLS]; HF card lists 0.2B params. Input: per paper 65 Hz, 6-s segments (zero-padded if shorter), detrend + Gaussian smoothing, each channel -> raw + 1st + 2nd derivative -> Mexican-hat CWT scales 1-64 stacked as RGB-like scalogram, patches 9x5; README example uses 64 Hz, 2 s, tensor [batch, nvar, samples], model.get_embedding(x, sampling_rate=64) -> [B, nvar, P, 768]. Pretraining: 9 public datasets (PPG, ECG, EEG, GSR, PCG, IMU), ~385 h raw expanded to 4,294 h (2.58M segments). Evaluation: linear probe (ridge for regression), 80/20 subject-stratified; 18 tasks / 11 datasets. Regression tasks: Noninvasive-BP, PPG-Hgb (hemoglobin), fetal HR; NormWear best on BP (92.42 score) but Chronos better on Hgb. Includes PPG-BP diabetes (DM) CLASSIFICATION among four PPG-BP tasks (HTN/DM/CVA/CVD) -- per-task numbers not extracted. Glucose regression: not evaluated.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Interesting because it already consumes 64 Hz input and builds a Mexican-hat CWT internally -- i.e. a pretrained version of our 2-D branch -- so a NormWear probe is a direct test of whether a large-scale-pretrained scalogram encoder carries glucose information that our from-scratch 2-D CNN could not. 0.2B params (~800 MB fp32) is fine on a 16 GB M4 for inference with small batches, but patch-level 768-d outputs need pooling before ridge. Apache-2.0.

findings.title: PPG-PT / 'HeartGPT' (Imperial, 2024) -- OPEN WEIGHTS, tiny decoder-only transformer, MIT
findings.source: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.20775 (html v2 https://arxiv.org/html/2407.20775v2). Code+checkpoints: https://github.com/harryjdavies/HeartGPT (MIT; Model_files/, zips PPGPT_500k_iters, ECGPT_560k_iters)
findings.summary: 443,493 params, 8 blocks, 8 heads, embedding dim 64. Input: PPG at 50 Hz, context 500 samples (10 s), signal scaled to 0-100 and rounded -> 101-token vocabulary. Pretraining: Capnobase (42 subj), BIDMC (53 subj), MIMIC-II cuffless-BP subset (~12k recordings); >128M tokens. Downstream: AF classification (LOSO AUC 0.93 for PPG), beat detection (F1 98%); no regression evaluated; no embedding-extraction API documented (fine-tuning example Heart_PT_finetune.py with layer freezing).
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Smallest and most interpretable, but pretraining corpus is tiny (~100 subjects + MIMIC-II subset) and no regression transfer evidence; token-level 64-d states would need pooling. Low priority; mention only if a 'small vs large pretraining' comparison is wanted.

findings.title: General time-series foundation models used as PPG baselines: MOMENT-1 and Chronos-2 -- OPEN WEIGHTS
findings.source: MOMENT: https://huggingface.co/AutonLab/MOMENT-1-large (MIT, ~0.3B params; also small/base; pip install momentfm, MOMENTPipeline.from_pretrained(..., model_kwargs={'task_name':'embedding'})). Chronos-2: https://huggingface.co/amazon/chronos-2 (Apache-2.0, ~120M, encoder-only, context up to 8192). Used as baselines in PaPaGei (arXiv 2410.20542), AnyPPG (2511.01747) and PPG-LM (2609.33516)
findings.summary: Both are generic univariate time-series encoders with open weights. In PaPaGei's regression suite MOMENT averaged MAE 10.43 vs PaPaGei-S 10.12 and beat PaPaGei on DaLiA HR (8.82 vs 11.53); Chronos 11.60. In PPG-LM's MC-MED glucose probe MOMENT-L and Chronos-2 scored R2 0.028-0.049 / 0.049-0.071 (two readings of the paper differ; see gaps), i.e. same band as the PPG-specific models.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Useful as a 'generic pretraining' control alongside PPG-specific encoders; MOMENT-large (~1.2 GB fp32) and Chronos-2 (~0.5 GB) both fit a 16 GB M4 for inference. MOMENT expects 512-sample inputs (not confirmed on the card; known from the MOMENT paper) so 5-s windows at ~100 Hz or 8-s at 64 Hz would be needed.

findings.title: PPG-LM (2026): ONLY published frozen-encoder linear-probe result for BLOOD GLUCOSE across open PPG foundation models -- all R2 < 0.09
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33516 (html v1 https://arxiv.org/html/2609.33516v1, Table 7 main text and Table 22 appendix D.7); dataset MC-MED https://physionet.org/content/mc-med/ (PhysioNet credentialed, DOI 10.13026/jz99-4j81, 118,385 ED visits / 70,545 patients, ECG+PPG+resp waveforms + lab results)
findings.summary: PPG-LM benchmarks PaPaGei-S, Pulse-PPG, AnyPPG, SIGMA-PPG, MOMENT-L and Chronos-2 with frozen representations and linear probes on MC-MED ED-visit labels, four 10-s windows per visit, including 'Glucose: blood glucose concentration, reflecting glycemic status at the sampled time' (first lab value of the visit). Reported glucose R2 (mean±SD): PaPaGei-S 0.032±0.007; Pulse-PPG 0.039±0.007 (main-text reading: 0.065); AnyPPG 0.065±0.008 (main-text reading: 0.041); SIGMA-PPG 0.041±0.009 (0.028); MOMENT-L 0.028±0.007 (0.049); Chronos-2 0.049±0.011 (0.071); PPG-LM Stage 2 0.083±0.011. Authors state glucose prediction 'remains weak'. Test split 3,612 patients / 5,196 visits / 1.1M windows. No sampling-rate detail for the baseline probes. PPG-LM's own weights/code: no release statement found.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: This is the strongest external corroboration of our negative result: with >50k-patient pretraining and tens of thousands of labelled ED visits, the best open PPG encoder explains <7% of glucose variance in a frozen probe. Cite it in Related Work/Discussion. It also identifies MC-MED as a large public (credentialed) PPG + lab-glucose resource -- a potential follow-up cohort far larger than Mendeley/BIG IDEAs (though 4.6+ TB-scale waveforms are not laptop-friendly).

findings.title: GPT-PPG (Emory, 2025) -- NO public weights
findings.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.08015 ; HF paper page https://huggingface.co/papers/2503.08015 lists no linked models; Emory preprint https://cs.emory.edu/~jyang71/files/gpt-ppg.pdf says code/weights 'will be published'
findings.summary: Decoder-only GPT models at 19M/85M/345M/1B params, pretrained on >200M 30-s PPG samples (private UCSF-derived data); AF detection and denoising; used as teacher in PPG-Distill (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2509.19215). No GitHub/HF checkpoint found; PPG-Distill's stated code URL https://github.com/LingFengGold/PPG-Distill returns 404 (checked via GitHub API).
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Not usable. Exclude; note that the 1B-parameter PPG model line has no open weights.

findings.title: SiamQuality (UCSF/Emory, Physiol. Meas. 2024) -- code only, NO released weights, private ICU pretraining data
findings.summary: SimSiam-style contrastive ResNet (ResNet50/101/152; 152 best) on 36M quality-paired 30-s PPG segments (UCSF ICU, 240 Hz downsampled to 40 Hz, min-max normalised, >600k h, ~21k patients). Data 'available on request'. Regression transfer: HR MAE 4.59 (TROIKA), 6.80 (DaLiA), 5.88 (WESAD); SBP MAE 8.6 mmHg (PulseDB, PPG-only); RR MAE 0.89 (BIDMC). Repo contains regression_train.py / simsiam_train.py but no checkpoint.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Not runnable as a frozen extractor without retraining. Cite as evidence that contrastive PPG pretraining transfers to HR/BP/RR regression; exclude from experiments.

findings.title: Apple (AHMS) wearable foundation models -- NO weights; Google LSM-1/LSM-2 -- NO weights; WavesFM -- NO weights
findings.source: Apple PPG/ECG: https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.05409 (ICLR 2024; HF page lists 0 linked models); Apple accelerometer-from-PPG distillation: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.11276; Apple behavioural WBM: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00191. Google LSM: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13638 ; LSM-2 blog https://research.google/blog/lsm-2-learning-from-incomplete-wearable-sensor-data/ (no weights/code/API mentioned). WavesFM: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09173 (6.8M h, 324k individuals; no release statement)
findings.summary: Apple's 2312.05409 trained PPG and ECG encoders on ~141k AHMS participants (~3 years) with contrastive SSL; no code/weights (internal data). 2412.11276 distils PPG encoders into accelerometry encoders (172k participants); no release. 2507.00191 uses 27 derived behavioural metrics, not raw PPG. Google LSM-2 (40M h, 60k persons, day-long windows on Fitbit/Pixel) -- blog gives no weights, code or API. WavesFM (two-stage segment/temporal encoder on PPG+accelerometry, 58 tasks) -- no release found.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: None of these can be run. They matter only for Related Work: the largest wearable PPG encoders are closed, so the open landscape is PaPaGei / Pulse-PPG / AnyPPG / SIGMA-PPG / NormWear.

findings.title: Other open items checked: CAP (code only), wavelet MMR (no release), PPG-VascularAge (task model, not an encoder)
findings.source: CAP https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15284 (code https://github.com/gody123gody/CAP, no weights statement); MMR https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12215 (17M segments from 32k smartwatch users, 19 tasks, no release statement); PPG-VascularAge https://huggingface.co/Ngks03/PPG-VascularAge (MIT, UK Biobank beat-averaged input, outputs one age value, no embedding API)
findings.summary: CAP: cross-modal PPG-EHR contrastive pretraining on MC-MED-derived text; respiratory-rate regression gain +87.6% rel.; no weights. MMR: masked wavelet-coefficient reconstruction transformer, 10-s PPG, smartwatch data; no weights. PPG-VascularAge: single-output model; third-party age benchmark shows it is worse than PaPaGei/Pulse-PPG as a probe (linear-probe MAE 9.72 vs 9.28 y).
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Exclude from experiments; optionally cite MMR/CAP as 2026 state of the art without open weights.

implications: Five open-weight PPG encoders can be run as frozen feature extractors on an M4 MacBook Air 16 GB without any training: PaPaGei-S (5.7M params, 23 MB, BSD-3 code / unlicensed weights, 125 Hz x 10 s), AnyPPG (~4M params, 16 MB, no license, 125 Hz x 10 s, 0.5-8 Hz), Pulse-PPG (28.5M, 315 MB zip, MIT, 50 Hz, variable length, no filtering), SIGMA-PPG (363 MB, no license, 50 Hz patches), NormWear (0.2B, Apache-2.0, 64/65 Hz x 6 s CWT). All are 1D-CNN or standard transformer ops that MPS supports; embedding our ~hundreds of Mendeley recordings and ~thousands of BIG IDEAs windows is a minutes-scale job, well inside the 20-min budget, and can run on CPU if MPS misbehaves.

Recommended experiment ('foundation-model probe'): for each encoder, extract one embedding per Mendeley recording (the raw 10-s recordings resampled to the model's rate are a single native segment for PaPaGei/AnyPPG) and per BIG IDEAs CGM reading (10 s or, for Pulse-PPG/SIGMA-PPG, up to 60-120 s pre-reading BVP already cached in sub_XXX.npz), then fit ridge (and optionally a small MLP) under the existing LOSO / chronological-with-guard protocols, reporting next to the train-mean and subject-mean nulls. Load every checkpoint with map_location='cpu' and weights_only=True where the pickle allows (SIGMA-PPG's pickle contains argparse.Namespace and may need weights_only=False -- treat as untrusted code).

This turns the paper's negative result from 'our small CNN trained on ~200 windows cannot beat the mean' (which a reviewer will attribute to under-training) into 'encoders pretrained on 57k-110k hours of PPG, probed with the same leakage-controlled protocol, cannot beat the mean either' -- a much stronger and more publishable claim, and it directly addresses the 'did you try a foundation model?' review question.

External corroboration already exists and should be cited: PPG-LM (arXiv 2609.33516) probed PaPaGei-S, Pulse-PPG, AnyPPG, SIGMA-PPG, MOMENT-L and Chronos-2 on MC-MED lab glucose (thousands of ED visits) and obtained R2 of only 0.03-0.08 for every model. No open PPG foundation model paper (PaPaGei, Pulse-PPG, AnyPPG, SIGMA-PPG, NormWear, SiamQuality) evaluates glucose regression; NormWear reports only PPG-BP diabetes classification.

Preprocessing must be re-derived from raw per encoder: PaPaGei needs 0.5-12 Hz Chebyshev + z-score at 125 Hz; AnyPPG 0.5-8 Hz + z-score at 125 Hz; Pulse-PPG wants unfiltered, person-level z-scored 50 Hz signals (person-level normalisation is leakage-safe only if computed on training-period data for BIG IDEAs); NormWear takes 64 Hz raw and builds its own derivatives/CWT. The current 64 Hz / 0.5-8 Hz / 5-s cache is not directly reusable except for NormWear.

Also report a generic-pretraining control (MOMENT-1-large or Chronos-2, both open, MIT/Apache) so the paper can say whether PPG-specific pretraining adds anything over generic time-series pretraining for glucose; PaPaGei's own paper shows MOMENT is competitive on several regression tasks.

Licensing/attribution for the paper: Pulse-PPG (MIT) and NormWear (Apache-2.0) are clean; PaPaGei weights carry no explicit license on Zenodo (code BSD-3); AnyPPG and SIGMA-PPG repos have no license at all -- usable for a research evaluation but do not redistribute their weights or derived embeddings; cite repositories and checkpoint DOIs/commits.

MC-MED on PhysioNet (credentialed; ECG/PPG waveforms + lab glucose for ~70k patients) is a much larger public cohort for leakage-controlled PPG->glucose work than Mendeley or BIG IDEAs; flag as future work (data scale is not laptop-friendly, but a subset of visits with glucose labels could be).

Not usable (no public weights): GPT-PPG (all four sizes), SiamQuality (code only, private data), Apple AHMS PPG/ECG and accelerometer models, Google LSM-1/LSM-2, WavesFM, PPG-LM, CAP, wavelet-MMR. The paper's Related Work can state that the largest wearable PPG encoders remain closed.
gaps_or_uncertainties: PPG-LM glucose R2 values differ between the two passes over the paper (main text vs appendix Table 22): e.g. Pulse-PPG 0.065 vs 0.039, AnyPPG 0.041 vs 0.065, MOMENT-L 0.049 vs 0.028, Chronos-2 0.071 vs 0.049. The safe statement is 'all models R2 between 0.03 and 0.08'; verify the exact per-model values against https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.33516 before quoting them in a table.

Pulse-PPG's native sampling rate is stated inconsistently in its own paper (100 Hz raw vs '4-minute 50 Hz segments'); downstream evaluation used 50 Hz. Its behaviour on 10-s inputs (vs 4-min pretraining) is undocumented and may be poor.

AnyPPG and SIGMA-PPG parameter counts were not stated anywhere; the 16 MB and 363 MB checkpoint sizes are the only size evidence. AnyPPG's README says checkpoints 'will be updated', so pin the commit hash.

PaPaGei weight license: the Zenodo record shows no license for the .pt files; only the GitHub code is BSD-3. Pulse-PPG's Zenodo record cites an IEEE Access DOI while the paper is in IMWUT -- record metadata is inconsistent.
The PPG-Distill code link (github.com/LingFengGold/PPG-Distill) returns 404; GPT-PPG weights remain unreleased as of this search.

NormWear's per-task PPG-BP diabetes (DM) classification number was not extracted; and its paper reports 65 Hz / 6 s while the README example uses 64 Hz / 2 s -- confirm the accepted input length before probing.

MPS feasibility is inferred from parameter counts and standard layer types; none of the repositories document Apple-silicon runs. Group convolutions (AnyPPG groups_width=16) and custom CWT code (NormWear optimized_cwt) are the most likely MPS pain points; fall back to CPU.
No open PPG foundation model has been evaluated on wrist BVP vs CGM; whether any of them transfers to Empatica E4 data is untested (Pulse-PPG, trained on wrist field PPG, is the best prior).

review:stats.lens: Methodology and statistics (sample size, CIs, seeds, significance vs null, protocol soundness, hyper-parameter fairness). Reviewed ieee_paper.tex in full, results/subject_cv_summary.json, results/bigideas_summary.json, results_macros.tex, run_subject_cv.py, run_bigideas_cv.py, ppg_data.py, make_results_macros.py, and re-analysed the released out-of-fold CSVs in results/ (subject-cluster bootstrap, Wilcoxon, between/within-subject decomposition). No training was run.
strengths: Protocol in the code matches the text: LOSO via LeaveOneGroupOut on subject (run_subject_cv.py:171), fresh model per fold, fixed 40-epoch budget, no early stopping, train-only label standardisation (train_fold, lines 86-87), recording-level averaging (recording_level, line 124). Mendeley 10 s at 64 Hz -> 3 windows at 50% overlap -> 201 windows, as stated.

BIG IDEAs guard gap is implemented as described: train = t < cut - 3600 s, test = t >= cut (run_bigideas_cv.py:55-56); egv_time is POSIX seconds (scripts/fetch_bigideas.py:18) and tests/test_integrity.py:71-75 asserts 300-s CGM spacing, so the hour is a real hour. Only pre-reading BVP is used (ppg_data.py:161-168).
All numbers flow from results/*.json through make_results_macros.py; no hand-typed numbers. Out-of-fold predictions are released per model and seed, which made independent re-analysis possible.

Three seeds on Mendeley for every network; null and classical baselines are reported next to every network; the Clarke zone-A-vs-null point is correct and the per-subject BIG IDEAs breakdown is useful.

The label-replication artefact finding is real and valuable (tests/test_integrity.py:85 asserts it), and the leakage-controlled negative result is the kind of correction the field needs. The core idea is publishable if the statistics are brought up to standard.
major_issues: M1. The headline BIG IDEAs claim ('no PPG model recovers any of the glycaemic excursions', abstract and Sec. 5.3) is tested with an unfair comparison. The null model is each subject's OWN train-period mean (run_bigideas_cv.py:60-64, i.e. it uses subject identity), while the networks are a single population model with no subject identifier, trained on a pooled-standardised target (train_fold uses y[tr].mean() over all subjects). The network is structurally unable to reproduce the subject offset the null gets for free. My decomposition of results/bigideas_within_1d_seed0.csv: between-subject r of the model's per-subject mean prediction vs per-subject mean glucose = +0.54 (2-D: +0.60, 3-D: +0.48), within-subject demeaned r = +0.09 (ridge +0.09, 2-D +0.08, 3-D +0.10); median within-subject SD of predictions 4.0 mg/dL vs 19.4 mg/dL for CGM. So the models partially learn subject offsets and nothing within-subject, but the paper never shows this; it only shows that an un-personalised model loses to a personalised constant (dMAE +1.66 mg/dL, subject-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [+0.50, +3.10]). A fair test needs a personalised arm (subject one-hot/embedding, or regress the residual y - subject_train_mean, or per-subject fine-tune), as in the dataset's source paper Bent et al. 2021 npj Digit. Med. 4:89, doi:10.1038/s41746-021-00465-w, which reported personalised wearable models with 'up to 84% and 87% accuracy' for excursion detection and value prediction and is not cited at all. Until that arm exists, the conclusion must be scoped to 'a population model without personalisation'.

M2. No confidence interval or significance test anywhere in the paper, yet the abstract says the fusion network is 'statistically indistinguishable from the train-mean predictor' and Sec. 5.1 says the 1-D CNN 'is the only model with a clear positive correlation'. The only uncertainty shown is SD over 3 seeds, which is model noise, not sampling uncertainty over 23 subjects. My subject-cluster bootstrap (5000 resamples of subjects) on the released CSVs: fusion dMAE vs train-mean = -0.24 [-1.6,+1.0], +0.08 [-1.5,+1.4], +0.40 [-1.1,+1.9] for seeds 0/1/2 (Wilcoxon p = 0.70, 0.89, 0.73); 1-D CNN dMAE = -1.94 [-3.4,-0.7] p=0.038, -1.18 [-2.9,+0.3] p=0.15, -0.84 [-2.6,+0.7] p=0.47; 3-seed ensemble -1.4 [-3.0,-0.02]. So the 1-D CNN MAE advantage is significant for one seed out of three, uncorrected, and the paper's 13.4+/-0.5 vs 14.7 framing hides that. The 1-D r = 0.32 does hold up (cluster-bootstrap CI [0.13,0.52] for all seeds), and that is the one defensible positive finding. 'Indistinguishable' also needs an equivalence framing: the CIs are +/-1.5 mg/dL wide, so the study can only exclude improvements of about 2 mg/dL over the null; state that minimum detectable effect explicitly instead of 'not meaningfully better'.

M3. Winner's-curse / multiple comparison: the 1-D CNN is selected post hoc as the best of 7 models x 3 seeds and then reported in the abstract as 'the best model'. With 8 model rows and no correction, one seed at p=0.038 is what one expects under the null. Either pre-register the 1-D CNN as the primary comparison, report a Holm/Bonferroni-adjusted result, or present it as exploratory.

M4. The train-mean predictor's Pearson r is -0.59 in results/subject_cv_summary.json (mean_seed0.pearson_r = -0.5934; R2 = -0.036) but is printed as '--' in Table I. That negative correlation is the known distributional bias of leave-one-out / small-fold CV (Austin, Pe'er, Korem, Science Advances 11(48):eadx6976, 2025, doi:10.1126/sciadv.adx6976): leaving a subject out shifts the training mean against the held-out label, so every model that regresses toward its training mean is pulled toward negative r and negative R2. Hiding the number rather than discussing it is a problem on its own, and it means pooled r / R2 across LOSO folds are not interpretable as 'variance explained' without this caveat. Report the null's r, cite the bias, and consider the rebalanced LOO correction or at least GroupKFold with larger folds as a sensitivity analysis.

M5. Hyper-parameter fairness undermines the 'fusion hurts' claim. One lr (1e-3), one epoch budget (40), one batch size (16), one weight decay for a ~550k-parameter fusion net and the much smaller single branches, on ~192 training windows per fold, with no augmentation and no per-model tuning. Sec. 5.1 states 'Adding the 2-D and 3-D views ... therefore hurts', which is a causal claim the design cannot support; the Limitations paragraph concedes this but the Results and Abstract do not. Scope the claim to 'under one shared untuned configuration' or run a small, leakage-safe budget sweep (nested within training folds) for lr/weight decay/epochs for each model.

M6. BIG IDEAs experiment is incomplete and single-seed: one seed for every network (bigideas_summary.json has only *_seed0), and the fusion row in Table II is entirely '--' (macros \bigFusion* fall back to providecommand placeholders). An IEEE Transactions table cannot ship an empty row for the paper's titular model; either run it or remove the row and the claim 'we did not evaluate the fusion network on this cohort because...' from a results table. Pooled per-reading n = 8664 is also not the effective sample size (5-min CGM readings are strongly autocorrelated); all BIG IDEAs uncertainty must be at subject level (16 clusters). The '13 of 16 subjects worse' count is fine but should carry a sign test (two-sided binomial p = 0.021).

M7. The within-subject evidence that actually supports the paper's claim is computed but not reported: within_subject_r_median = 0.043 (1-D), 0.033 (2-D), 0.028 (3-D), 0.045 (ridge) in bigideas_summary.json, and the between/within decomposition in M1. Sec. 5.3 asserts the pooled r 'is entirely explained by between-subject differences' without showing any analysis. Put the per-subject r distribution (with cluster-bootstrap CI) and the decomposition in Table II; that is the result.

M8. Both dataset citations are wrong. The Mendeley dataset (doi:10.17632/37pm7jk7jn.1, https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/37pm7jk7jn/1) is by Ali Kermani and Hossein Esmaeili, not 'D. Kumar, V. Kumar, S. Chaudhary'; the page also lists 68 label files against 67 signal files, which the paper should reconcile (ppg_data.py:118-121 skips signals without labels but not labels without signals). The PhysioNet BIG IDEAs v1.1.3 DOI 10.13026/aw6y-fc44 is correct (https://physionet.org/content/big-ideas-glycemic-wearable/1.1.3/, published 13 Apr 2026, change: 'Updated misaligned food log dates') but the recommended citation is Cho, Kim, Bent, Dunn (2026), not 'B. Bent, M. Cho, A. Wittmann et al.'. Also the Mendeley dataset is at version 3 (doi:10.17632/37pm7jk7jn.3, same 67 signals / 23 subjects); state which version was used.

M9. Missing prior LOSO work on the same 23-subject dataset: Syamsul and Kim, Front. Bioeng. Biotechnol. 14:1843361, 2026, doi:10.3389/fbioe.2026.1843361 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13375809/) report MAE 11.59 mg/dL, RMSE 15.40, r = 0.83 on Kermani and Esmaeili's data with a subject-level split and no null baseline, and their 1D-CNN baseline gives MAE 13.45, which is almost exactly this paper's 1-D CNN (13.4). That paper is the ideal foil for the reporting argument in Sec. 6 and its absence weakens the related-work and novelty case; the reviewer will ask why the proposed protocol gives r = 0.32 where they report 0.83.

M10. Reference-noise floor is never stated, so 'no model beats the null' cannot be interpreted. Mendeley labels come from an Accu-Chek Active meter (dataset page), whose ISO 15197:2013 tolerance is 95% within +/-15 mg/dL (<100) or +/-15% (>=100), i.e. a label-noise MAE floor of several mg/dL on a 115 +/- 19 mg/dL cohort; Dexcom G6 MARD is 9.0% (Shah et al., Diabetes Technol. Ther. 20(6):428-433, 2018, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6422005), so the BIG IDEAs null MARD of 12.8% is within ~4 points of the reference's own error. Report these floors next to the null and the models.
minor_issues: BIG IDEAs windows: only the last 2 x 5 s of the 60 s of pre-reading BVP are used (--max-per-egv default 2, run_bigideas_cv.py:77; loader keeps up to 12). Ten seconds of wrist BVP under free living per 5-min CGM reading, with no motion-artefact rejection beyond finiteness and SD > 1e-3 (ppg_data.py:168) and no accelerometer gating, is a weak probe; the negative claim should be scoped to this window length or a longer-context ablation added. Interstitial lag (5-15 min) is also not discussed.

Per-window z-scoring (ppg_data.py:102-105) removes DC level and pulsatile amplitude, i.e. perfusion-related information that is among the most physiologically plausible glucose correlates. Justify or add an un-normalised-amplitude feature to the ridge baseline.

RidgeCV default (run_subject_cv.py:117) uses efficient leave-one-out at WINDOW level, and Mendeley windows overlap 50% within a recording, so the alpha selection leaks across overlapping windows of the same recording. Use GroupKFold by recording for alpha. The text 'chosen by leave-one-out on the training fold' should say window-level.

R2 is computed against the pooled mean of all 67 recordings (metrics(), line 135), which includes the held-out labels; state this, and note that the null's R2 of -0.04 (not 0) is the LOSO bias from M4.

within_subject_r_median on Mendeley (JSON) is computed on subjects with >2 recordings, i.e. a handful of 3-7 point correlations; values like 0.65 (3d_seed0) and -0.29 (fusion_seed1) are noise. Fine to omit from the paper, but do not let them leak into the released summary without a caveat.
Docstring of run_subject_cv.py says 'cosine LR'; code and paper say one-cycle (OneCycleLR). Trivial, but the code is cited as the artifact.
Table I footnote uses \mendFusionSeeds for all networks; fine today (all 3) but fragile. Table II lacks A+B and lacks n per subject; Fig. 4b should show per-subject CI bars.
Sec. 3.1 says 'Kumar et al.' and '7 female, 16 male'; the Syamsul and Kim paper says 15 male / 8 female for the same dataset; verify against the label files.

bibitem li2020ecg is cited for 'wavelet scalograms' but is a sleep-staging CNN-LSTM paper; cite a scalogram/CWT reference. hina2021noninvasive is cited as 'Hina and Saadeh, Sensors 2022' with key 2021; harmonise.

The sign test for 'worse for 13 of 16 subjects' (p = 0.021) and the subject-cluster bootstrap I ran are cheap; add a stats paragraph to Sec. 4.4 and a scripts/stats.py so these numbers are generated, not hand-typed.
what_would_change_my_verdict: A personalised arm on BIG IDEAs (subject embedding / residual-over-subject-mean / per-subject fine-tune) for at least the 1-D CNN and the fusion net, 3 seeds, with within-subject r and per-subject dMAE vs the subject-mean null reported with subject-cluster bootstrap CIs. If that arm also fails to beat the null, the headline claim stands and is strong; if it does not, the paper's conclusion changes.

Subject-level 95% CIs (cluster bootstrap over the 23 / 16 subjects) on every MAE, dMAE-vs-null and r in Tables I and II, plus a stated minimum detectable improvement over the null, replacing seed-SD as the uncertainty.
Explicit handling of the LOSO distributional bias: report the null's r and R2, cite Austin et al. 2025, and add a GroupKFold (e.g. 5-fold by subject) sensitivity row showing the 1-D CNN r survives.
A pre-specified primary comparison (1-D CNN vs train-mean) with multiplicity correction for the rest, or an explicit 'exploratory' label on the 1-D CNN advantage.
Either a leakage-safe per-model budget sweep (nested in training folds) or rewording of every 'fusion hurts' / 'adds variance' sentence to 'under one shared configuration'.

Table II completed (fusion run, >=3 seeds) or the fusion row removed; corrected dataset citations (Kermani and Esmaeili; Cho, Kim, Bent, Dunn); Bent et al. 2021 and Syamsul and Kim 2026 discussed in Related Work and Discussion; reference-noise floors (ISO 15197, G6 MARD 9.0%) stated next to the nulls.

review:novelty.lens: Novelty and impact for an IEEE Transactions audience (TBME / JBHI / Sensors J): is the artefact finding new, is a negative result on 23+16 subjects enough, what is missing to make this a reference benchmark. Based on full read of ieee_paper.tex, results/subject_cv_summary.json, results/bigideas_summary.json, results_macros.tex, run_subject_cv.py, run_bigideas_cv.py, ppg_data.py, tests/test_integrity.py, the local Archive_Dataset files, and the literature checks cited below (no training run).
major_issues: NOVELTY OF THE CENTRAL MESSAGE IS ALREADY TAKEN (concurrent/prior work not cited). Ramesh, Neufeld, Küttner, Röddiger, Beigl (KIT), 'Reassessing the Feasibility of PPG-Based Non-Invasive Blood Glucose Level Estimation', arXiv:2608.01820 (3 Aug 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01820, code github.com/R-Supraja/bgl-evaluation-pipeline) re-implements five published PPG-glucose methods (Zeynali 2025 ResNet-34, Alghlayini 2023 1D-CNN, Prabha 2022 MFCC+XGBoost, Islam 2021 PLS, Gupta 2021 XGBoost) on VitalDB (4,626 participants) under random / participant-aware / leave-some-participants-out splits with a train-mean baseline, finds R2 ~0 or negative for all under LSPO, and explicitly concludes that Clarke zones A+B >90% for every model AND the mean baseline 'systematically conceal model failure'. They also use the same MUST/Mendeley 23-subject dataset as an OOD test set (global-mean baseline MAE 16.0, zone A 77.6%; Islam PLS trained on VitalDB reaches MAE 13.37 / zone A 86.6% on MUST without ever seeing it). The draft's contributions 2, 3 and the 'Clarke grid is uninformative without a null model' point are therefore not new to the field, and the draft's best number (1-D CNN LOSO MAE 13.4) is matched by a feature model that never trained on the dataset. Separately, Seyedebrahimi, Ojeda, Zarrintaj, 'A Leakage-Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Sensor Fusion for Wrist-Worn Glucose Estimation', medRxiv 10.64898/2026.08.03.26359550 (4 Aug 2026, code github.com/mirmehdi/physiofusion) already reports on BIG IDEAs (PhysioNet v1.1.2, 15 subjects, subject-grouped 5-fold CV) that wristband-only models (PPG+EDA+TEMP+ACC) give RMSE 22.58 vs 22.63 for time-of-day-only and 22.76 for train-mean, i.e. 'wrist signals carry no glucose information beyond the cohort mean'. The draft's Sec. VI-C conclusion is the same finding with a different split. Neither paper is cited; the Related Work section (11 references, several unverifiable) does not position the paper against either. A Transactions reviewer who runs one Google Scholar search will find both.

THE ARTEFACT FINDING IS NEW BUT ITS CLAIMED IMPACT IS UNSUPPORTED. The 'widely circulated derivative' is identifiable: the local Archive_Dataset/clean-dataset.csv (46,758,588 bytes; header PPG_Signal,Patient_Id,Heart_Rate,Systolic_Peak,Diastolic_Peak,Pulse_Area,index,Gender,Age,Glucose_level,Height,Weight,pl) matches the Kaggle dataset 'PPG signal with Blood sugar level data' by muhammadyasirsaleem (clean-dataset.csv 46.76 MB, https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/muhammadyasirsaleem/ppg-signal-with-blood-sugar-level-data; companion repo https://github.com/yasirsaleem502/Predict-Blood-Glucose-Level-Based-on-PPG-Signals fits polynomial regression to it). The paper never names the source, never quotes the 'pl' column that is the label-index of the cross-join (rows 0 and 1 share PPG_Signal=511 with Glucose_level 99 then 102, pl 1 then 2), and claims 'judging by its column layout, for other published models' without a single citation. An extended search for papers using the Kaggle column names found none; every peer-reviewed paper that uses this cohort (Zeynali et al., Sci Rep 15:581, 2025, doi:10.1038/s41598-024-84265-8; Kermani & Esmaeili, BioImpacts 15:30589, 2025, doi:10.34172/bi.30589; Rizal & Kim, Front. Bioeng. Biotechnol. 2026, doi:10.3389/fbioe.2026.1843361; Ramesh et al. 2026) works from the raw Mendeley .mat/.csv files. So the artefact, as documented, invalidates the authors' own earlier draft (legacy_ieee_paper_v1.tex) and Kaggle notebooks, not the published literature. Either demonstrate that a published result depends on this file (cite it, reproduce the 0.07 mg/dL oracle on their protocol) or drop the 'other published models' claim; as a contribution it is then a paragraph plus a unit test, not a Transactions headline.

THE BIG IDEAs COMPARISON IS STRUCTURALLY UNFAIR TO THE MODELS, SO THE HEADLINE NEGATIVE ('no PPG model beats each subject's own mean') IS NOT ESTABLISHED. run_bigideas_cv.py trains ONE population network on all subjects' training periods with no subject identifier and no per-subject offset (train_fold standardises y with the pooled training mean/sd), then compares it with subject_mean_baseline(), which is given subject identity plus each subject's training-period mean. The ridge baseline likewise is a global RidgeCV with no subject indicator. The null model therefore has information the models never receive. The per-subject table in bigideas_summary.json shows exactly this: the 1-D CNN's per-subject MAE tracks the subject-mean MAE almost one-for-one (001: 13.06 vs 12.20; 010: 20.93 vs 22.02; 013: 23.10 vs 16.18) because the network is forced to predict a cohort-level value. The clinically relevant question (does PPG add information on top of a personal baseline?) requires at minimum: (a) target = glucose minus subject training mean (residual learning) or subject mean as an input feature, (b) per-subject fine-tuning / per-subject models, (c) a persistence/last-value baseline and a time-of-day baseline (Seyedebrahimi et al. show time-of-day alone equals wrist-only). Without (a)-(c) the sentence in the abstract 'no PPG model recovers any of the glycaemic excursions' is a statement about the experimental design, not about PPG.

NO STATISTICS SUPPORT THE WORDS 'STATISTICALLY INDISTINGUISHABLE' (abstract) OR 'NOT MEANINGFULLY BETTER' (contribution 3). metrics() in run_subject_cv.py computes point estimates only; there is no confidence interval, no paired test, no cluster bootstrap over the 23 subjects, no permutation test, and no power / minimum-detectable-effect analysis. With n=67 recordings (23 clusters, 1-7 recordings each; subject 12 has one recording) the 1-D CNN's MAE 13.4+/-0.5 vs train-mean 14.7 and r=0.32+/-0.02 (p~0.008 for n=67 if treated as independent, which they are not) may or may not be a real effect, and the paper simultaneously calls it 'the best model' and 'not meaningfully better'. The per-fold log (results_loso_seed0.log) shows held-out-subject MAE ranging 6.1-34.8 mg/dL, so the pooled MAE is dominated by subjects 13 and 18 (183 mg/dL readings). Required: subject-level cluster bootstrap CIs for MAE/RMSE/r for every model, paired comparison model-vs-mean on per-recording absolute errors with subject clustering, per-subject results table, and the within-subject r that the code already computes (within_subject_r_median = 0.07 / 0.04 / 0.003 for the 1-D CNN across seeds, i.e. the r=0.32 is entirely between-subject) but the paper never reports. The LOSO train-mean's r = -0.59 (a known property of leave-one-group-out mean predictors) is hidden as '--' in Table I instead of explained.

THE MANUSCRIPT IS INCOMPLETE AND CONTAINS FACTUAL/CITATION ERRORS A REVIEWER WILL CATCH. (i) Table II has a '1D+2D+3D cross-attention' row whose six cells are the '--' fallback macros; README says the fusion run on BIG IDEAs is 'not in the paper yet'. A table row with no data cannot go to review. (ii) Sec. III-A says '7 female, 16 male'; the raw label files give 15 male / 8 female (checked over all 67 label_*.csv; Ramesh et al. report the same 15 M / 8 F). (iii) The Mendeley dataset is attributed to 'D. Kumar, V. Kumar, S. Chaudhary'; the actual authors are Ali Kermani and Hossein Esmaeili, University of Science and Technology of Mazandaran, Iran (https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/37pm7jk7jn; v4 doi:10.17632/37pm7jk7jn.4, 10 Sep 2025; IEEE DataPort mirror doi:10.21227/mekr-0a81; source article doi:10.34172/bi.30589). (iv) BIG IDEAs v1.1.3 is attributed to 'B. Bent, M. Cho, A. Wittmann, et al.'; PhysioNet's citation is Cho, P., Kim, J., Bent, B., Dunn, J. (2026), doi:10.13026/aw6y-fc44 (https://physionet.org/content/big-ideas-glycemic-wearable/1.1.3/), and the original study Bent et al., npj Digit. Med. 4:89, 2021, doi:10.1038/s41746-021-00465-w is not cited at all even though it reports, on the same 16 subjects, a personalised XGBoost (first 50% train / rest test) RMSE 21.10+/-4.50 and LOPO RMSE 21.22+/-4.14 that 'beat naive mean and median baselines' using E4 features plus food logs. The draft must engage with that claim (PPG-only vs multimodal+food) rather than ignore it. (v) 'dinh2022ppg' (Dinh, Nguyen, Nguyen, Tran, 'Non-invasive blood glucose estimation using photoplethysmography and deep learning', Proc. IEEE Int. Conf. Biomed. Eng., 2022) and 'li2020ecg' (X. Li et al., 'Automatic staging of sleep disorders using a multi-scale CNN-LSTM architecture', IEEE TNSRE 28(10), 2020) could not be found in any index; both look fabricated and the latter is cited as the source for wavelet scalograms of PPG. 'hina2021noninvasive' is a NIR-spectroscopy review (Hina & Saadeh, Sensors 22(13):4855, 2022, doi:10.3390/s22134855), not a source for 'hand-crafted pulse features ... MAE 15-25 mg/dL'. (vi) PhysioNet's inclusion criteria state 'including only post-menopausal females' for BIG IDEAs; the draft says '16 adults'. Verify against Demographics.csv in the zip and state sex. (vii) Sec. III-C/IV-A text says BIG IDEAs windows come from 'the 10 s before the reading'; load_bigideas() takes the last two gap-free 5-s windows anywhere in a 60-s lookback (lookback_s=60, max_windows_per_egv=2), so a window can be up to 60 s before the reading.

ONE HOME-GROWN NETWORK ON 201 WINDOWS IS NOT A BENCHMARK. The 1D-2D-3D cross-attention net (548,801 parameters) is trained on ~192 windows per fold; its failure says nothing about multi-view PPG representations and the paper admits as much (Sec. VI, Limitations). The field's actual claims (Zeynali 2025: ResNet-34, MUST RMSE 19.7 / zone A 76.6% when trained on VitalDB; Kermani & Esmaeili 2025: SVR on SDF-MFCC, RMSE 26.01, 99.3% zone A on their own dataset; Rizal & Kim 2026: attention CNN-GRU, MAE 11.59 / r 0.83 on this cohort with an inconsistent split description; Soliman et al. arXiv:2411.11094 CNN-GRU MAE 2.96 / R2 0.97 with no split described) are the ones a reviewer wants tested under the leakage-controlled protocol. Ramesh et al. did that for five methods; this draft tests none of them. Per-window z-scoring (ppg_data._zscore_rows) also discards absolute amplitude / AC-DC ratio, so handcrafted_features' log total power is near-constant and the ridge baseline is weakened by design; meta['raw_std'] is computed but never used. The negative result is conditional on preprocessing choices the paper does not ablate.

SAMPLE SIZE AND COHORT: 23 non-diabetic subjects / 67 fingerprick readings (88-183 mg/dL, 44 of 67 within one SD of the mean) and 16 non-diabetic (HbA1c 5.2-6.4%) wrist-worn subjects cannot support a general claim about 'how much glucose information a single PPG channel carries'. The title promises a quantity; the paper delivers two small negative experiments without CIs. For a Transactions audience the acceptable framings are (a) a reproducible multi-dataset benchmark with frozen folds and a leaderboard, or (b) a methods/pitfalls paper with a formal leakage taxonomy and detection tests validated on several public datasets. The present draft is neither.
minor_issues: Table I prints '--' for the train-mean r; the JSON value is -0.59 (LOSO mean predictor is anti-correlated by construction). Report it and explain in one sentence; also report R2 relative to the pooled mean next to a note that it penalises the null model.
Mendeley networks use 3 seeds but all BIG IDEAs networks use 1 seed (bigideas_summary.json has only *_seed0); the paper's 'mean +/- std over seeds' claim does not apply to Table II.
run_subject_cv.py docstring says 'cosine LR'; code and paper say OneCycleLR. Fix the docstring.

Sec. III-A reports 'subjects contributed between one and seven recordings'; give the full distribution (1,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,3,3,3,3,3,3,4,4,5,6,7 - 12 of 23 subjects have <=2 recordings), since within-subject r is undefined for most of them.
The Mendeley citation should point to the version actually downloaded (archive (2)/PPG_Dataset) and note the DOI of that version; v4 (2025) lists 68 label files vs 67 raw files.

Fig. 2 caption (artefact): also quote the Kaggle 'pl' column and row count so a reader can reproduce the check without the file; tests/test_integrity.py reads only the first 20,000 rows of the first patient, which is fine as a smoke test but is not the 'asserts the cycling pattern' claimed in Sec. III-B.

IEEEtran: \markboth says 'IEEE Transactions (preprint)'. Name the target journal; TBME and JBHI have different length and abstract rules (JBHI structured abstract ~250 words; the current abstract is ~270).
Zone A for the fusion model is reported as the 'lowest of all models (78.6%)' as evidence it 'adds variance' - on n=67 that is 5 recordings; say so.

The 1-h guard gap is applied on the training side only (tr: t < cut-3600; te: t >= cut). That is correct but the text 'readings in the hour before the cut discarded' should say they are dropped from training, not from the evaluation.
Reference 'almarshad2021' is keyed 2021 but is the 2022 Healthcare review; 'hina2021noninvasive' likewise keyed 2021 for a 2022 paper. Harmless but sloppy.
IDF Diabetes Atlas 10th ed. 2021 (537 million) is fine; the 11th edition (2025) gives ~589 million and will be what reviewers expect in a 2026 submission.
strengths: The label-replication/cross-join artefact in the Kaggle 'clean-dataset.csv' derivative is genuinely new: no paper or Kaggle discussion found documents it, and the mechanism (per-sample x per-label join, 'pl' index column, window mean collapsing to subject mean, per-subject oracle MAE 0.07 mg/dL) is correctly diagnosed and reproducible from the local file header.

The protocol in code is sound and matches the text in the places that matter: LOSO with subject-disjoint folds (tests/test_integrity.py::test_loso_folds_never_leak_subjects), train-only label standardisation, fixed epoch budget with no early stopping, recording-level aggregation, chronological split with a 1-h training-side guard on BIG IDEAs, Dexcom Low/High excluded, pre-reading windows only. The macro pipeline (results/*.json -> results_macros.tex) guarantees the paper carries no hand-typed numbers.
Withdrawing the earlier 6.89 mg/dL / 98.9% zone A result in print and keeping legacy_ieee_paper_v1.tex as a record is the right thing to do and is rare.

Releasing out-of-fold predictions per reference measurement (results/*.csv) is exactly what a benchmark needs; the within_subject_r_median field already in the JSON is the most informative statistic the paper has and should be promoted to the tables.

The 'Clarke zone A is a cohort property' argument is correct and the numbers (constant predictor 83.6% zone A on Mendeley, 78.8% on BIG IDEAs) are a useful calibration point even though Ramesh et al. made the same point first.
what_would_change_my_verdict: Reframe as a reference benchmark and cite/position against Ramesh et al. 2026 (arXiv:2608.01820) and Seyedebrahimi et al. 2026 (medRxiv 10.64898/2026.08.03.26359550) and Bent et al. 2021 (doi:10.1038/s41746-021-00465-w): state precisely what is added (LOSO on MUST itself with multi-seed nets; within-subject chronological split with guard gap on BVP-only; the Kaggle artefact and its test).

Add datasets until the claim is population-level, with frozen fold files shipped in the repo: VitalDB PPG+glucose (4,626 participants; the standard in Zeynali 2025 and Ramesh 2026), PhysioCGM (Sci Data 2025, doi:10.1038/s41597-025-06090-6, 10 T1D participants, multimodal), the Zenodo ePPG dataset (doi:10.5281/zenodo.21978226, 24 participants incl. 3 T1D, 125 records, 6-channel 530/655/940 nm at 100 Hz), BIG IDEAs all 16 subjects with ACC/EDA/TEMP (already in sub_XXX.npz) so the PPG-only vs multimodal question Bent raised is answered, plus the Kaggle derivative as a documented 'do not use' negative control.

Re-implement at least three published methods (Zeynali ResNet-34 1-s segments, Islam PLS features, Kermani SDF-MFCC+SVR, Rizal attention CNN-GRU) under the leakage-controlled protocol instead of only the home-grown fusion net; the fusion net becomes one row, not the subject of the paper.

Fix the BIG IDEAs design: residual-to-subject-mean targets or subject-mean input, per-subject fine-tuning, persistence and time-of-day baselines, >=3 seeds, and run the fusion model so Table II has no empty row. Report per-subject MAE deltas with CIs.

Add inferential statistics everywhere: subject-level cluster bootstrap CIs, paired model-vs-null tests on per-recording absolute errors, within-subject r in every table, a minimum-detectable-effect calculation for n=67/23 and n=8,664/16, and a positive-control experiment (e.g. heart rate or subject-identity recovery from the same windows) proving the pipeline can learn something.

Ablate the preprocessing choices the negative result depends on: per-window z-scoring vs amplitude-preserving normalisation (use meta['raw_std'] / AC-DC ratio), 5-s vs 10-s windows, 0.5-8 Hz vs wider band, 64 Hz vs native rate on Mendeley.

Correct every citation error listed above (Kermani & Esmaeili for Mendeley; Cho/Kim/Bent/Dunn 2026 doi:10.13026/aw6y-fc44 for BIG IDEAs v1.1.3; remove or replace dinh2022ppg and li2020ecg; 15 M / 8 F; verify BIG IDEAs sex from Demographics.csv), name the Kaggle source of the derivative, and either evidence or delete the claim that other published models used it.

If the above is done, the natural venues are IEEE JBHI or IEEE Sensors Journal (both have accepted leakage/evaluation papers, e.g. the 2023 IEEE Sensors J. paper on data leakage in PPG/ECG blood-pressure estimation, https://www.aminer.org/pub/648b8b45d68f896efad69fea) or IEEE OJEMB for a benchmark/data-descriptor; TBME would expect the multi-dataset, multi-method version.

sweep:leakage.angle: EVALUATION PITFALLS: data leakage, subject-wise vs record-wise splits, over-optimistic physiological-signal ML, prior critiques of PPG-glucose results and the Mendeley/Kaggle PPG-glucose dataset, reporting standards (TRIPOD+AI, PROBAST+AI, CONSORT-AI, DECIDE-AI, NERVE-ML), and quantified leakage inflation ("leakage ladder").

findings.title: Reassessing the Feasibility of PPG-Based Non-Invasive Blood Glucose Level Estimation (Ramesh, Neufeld, Kuettner, Roeddiger, Beigl; KIT)
findings.source: Proc. 2026 ACM Int. Symp. Wearable Computers (ISWC/UbiComp '26), pp. 127-133, DOI 10.1145/3830727.3834821; preprint arXiv:2608.01820 (https://arxiv.org/html/2608.01820v1)
findings.summary: Re-implements five published PPG->glucose methods (Zeynali 2025 ResNet-34; Alghlayini 2023 1D-CNN; Prabha 2022 MFCC+XGBoost; Islam 2021 PLS; Gupta 2021 XGBoost) on VitalDB (4,626 participants, glucose 44-525 mg/dL) under three split protocols plus an out-of-distribution test on the 'MUST' dataset, which is the Mendeley 37pm7jk7jn set (23 participants, 67 sessions, 2175 Hz, glucose 88-183 mg/dL, cited to Kermani & Esmaeili 2023). Table 2: train-mean baseline MAE 26.40, R2 0.00, CEG A+B 52.0%. Zeynali ResNet-34: random window-level split MAE 13.97, R2 0.60, MARD 12.1%, CEG 82.2%; participant-aware split MAE 36.18, R2 -0.08; leave-some-participants-out MAE 25.93, R2 -0.04 (i.e. equal to the mean baseline). All other methods: R2 between -0.12 and 0.05 under participant-aware/LSPO. On MUST (OOD): baseline MAE 16.00, R2 -0.08, A+B 77.6%; models MAE 13.4-18.2, R2 -0.06 to -0.34, A+B 62.7-86.6%. Conclusions: random window-level splits overestimate generalisation via sample-level leakage; '>90% of predictions in Clarke A+B including the baseline' so clinical-zone metrics 'systematically conceal model failure'; recommends participant-aware and LSPO protocols, a dedicated validation set, a mean-prediction baseline, and reporting MAE/R2 alongside CEG. Each glucose label is attached to a 16-min PPG segment whose sub-windows inherit the label; no augmentation used.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Closest prior work and must be cited; it partially pre-empts the 'random splits inflate PPG-glucose' and 'Clarke zone A is uninformative without a null model' points. It does NOT describe the label-replication artefact in the derivative CSV, does not run LOSO on the Mendeley raw recordings as a primary experiment, and does not test within-subject tracking against CGM. Its MUST OOD numbers (baseline MAE 16.0, A+B 77.6%) are a direct external sanity check for our Mendeley train-mean baseline. Its Table 2 is a ready-made leakage ladder (random -> participant-aware -> LSPO -> OOD) to quote.

findings.title: Referee report (Pith, AI-generated) on Soliman et al., 'Non-Invasive Glucose Level Monitoring from PPG using a Hybrid CNN-GRU Deep Learning Network'
findings.summary: Paper trains on the Mazandaran/Mendeley dataset (67 signals, 23 participants, glucose 88-187 mg/dL), augments 67 -> 269 signals with Gaussian noise BEFORE shuffling and splitting, splits at signal level, and reports MAE 2.96 mg/dL, R2 0.97 and 100% Clarke zone A. The report flags augmentation-before-split leakage, no participant-independent split, no participant IDs, 10-fold CV MAE (~1.77) inconsistent with headline numbers, and that 100% zone A on a narrow 88-187 mg/dL range is 'not a valid safety indicator'; recommends desk rejection and subject-independent splits with augmentation applied only inside training folds.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Concrete, citable example of the exact pipeline errors on the same dataset we use; supports our claim that sub-10 mg/dL MAE reports on this data are artefacts of evaluation. Note the source is an automated review, not peer review; cite as such or cite the underlying paper's stated protocol.

findings.title: Non-invasive blood glucose monitoring using PPG signals with various deep learning models and implementation using TinyML (Zeynali, Alipour, Tarvirdizadeh, Ghamari)
findings.summary: Trains ResNet-34/VGG16/CNN-LSTM on VitalDB (6,388 subjects) with 1-s segments; the split is explicitly at segment level: 'we use 70% of the segments for training, 15% for validation, and the remaining 15% for testing'. Reports RMSE 19.7, MAE 14.8 mg/dL, Clarke zone A 76.6% / B 23.4% ('100% clinically acceptable'). Uses the Mendeley/MUST data as an external test but calls the 67 recordings '67 testing subjects' (the dataset has 23 subjects). No mean-prediction baseline. Ramesh et al. 2026 re-ran this model and found R2 drops from 0.60 (random) to -0.04 (LSPO).
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Example of a recent high-visibility paper on the same datasets with segment-level leakage and a recording/subject confusion; its re-evaluation by Ramesh et al. is the published 'ladder' for this exact model. Cite in Related Work as the kind of result our protocol is designed to test.

findings.title: Interpretable non-invasive glucose monitoring: an attention-based deep learning framework for visualizing hemodynamic correlates in PPG signals (Syamsul & Kim)
findings.summary: Uses the Mendeley 23-subject dataset (348 segments of 40 s), subject-level split 16/3/4 subjects; reports MAE 11.59, RMSE 15.40, Pearson r 0.83 on 4 test subjects for an attention-GRU vs 1D-CNN MAE 13.45 / r 0.75. Single split, no seeds, no null/mean baseline, no LOSO; internal inconsistencies (Sec. 5.2 mentions LOSO, Sec. 7.5 says no subject-independent evaluation performed; Bland-Altman bias reported as +0.12 in text and 108.30 in figure caption).
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: The only prior Mendeley-dataset paper found with a subject-level split; its r=0.83 on four held-out subjects contrasts with our LOSO result and illustrates why single small held-out sets without a null model are unreliable (Varoquaux +/-10% error bars). Worth citing and contrasting directly.

findings.title: 90% Accuracy for PPG-Based Non-Invasive Blood Glucose Prediction by Deep Learning with Cohort Arrangement and Quarterly Measured HbA1c (Chu et al.)
findings.summary: 2,538 volunteers, two 1-min PPG recordings each; ten random 9:1 train/test splits, not stated to be by subject. Adding HbA1c as an input feature raises Clarke zone A from 60.6% to 76.9% overall and 86.6% -> 94.2% in the no-medication cohort (MAE 8.9 mg/dL). The paper does not analyse within-subject tracking. The empirical.health post interprets this as PPG models learning each subject's baseline (HbA1c, age, BMI) rather than glucose dynamics and reports accuracy collapsing to ~60% at scale.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Supports our discussion that cross-subject 'accuracy' is largely between-subject baseline estimation (demographics/HbA1c), which is why our demographics-only ridge baseline belongs in the table. The blog is secondary; cite Chu et al. for the numbers and frame the baseline interpretation as ours.

findings.title: How to Demonstrate the Glucose Specificity of a Non-Invasive CGM: A Case Study of the SKAMo-2 Clinical Trial and Neogly (Blanc, Blandin, Coutard, Jourde, Marie, Benhamou)
findings.summary: Argues MARD, Clarke/Parkes grids and ISO 15197 agreement rates presume glucose specificity rather than test it. Proposes five controls: signal-quality gating before benchmarking; a white-noise control (an algorithm trained on pure Gaussian noise reached MARD 25% on short test windows); a constant-glycaemia control to expose trial-duration bias; a sensor-ablation control; and explicit reporting of the generalisation level (intra-experimentation / intra-patient / inter-patient). Reports naive constant model MARD 55% vs DNN 37% on inter-patient splits in 8 T1D participants, stating any MARD is uninterpretable in isolation.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Independent, device-industry statement of our central reporting recommendation (null model next to every metric; state the split level). Their three-level generalisation taxonomy maps onto our LOSO (inter-patient) and chronological-within-subject (intra-patient) protocols. A white-noise or label-shuffle control would strengthen our paper.

findings.title: Mendeley PPG-glucose dataset: 'The dataset of photoplethysmography signals collected from a pulse sensor to measure blood glucose level' (Kermani & Esmaeili, University of Science and Technology of Mazandaran)
findings.summary: 67 raw PPG signals from 23 individuals, 2175 Hz, 550-nm green pulse sensor with APDS-9008 photodiode, Accu-Chek Active reference; labels: participant ID, gender, age, glucose, height, weight; CC BY 4.0. Landing page lists contributors Ali Kermani and Hossein Esmaeili. RawData has 67 .mat/.csv files but Labels folder has 68 files (unexplained). Ramesh et al. 2026 and Zeynali et al. 2025 both cite it as 'Kermani & Esmaeili (2023)'.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Our draft's bibitem 'ppgdataset2023' credits 'D. Kumar, V. Kumar, S. Chaudhary' and v1; the dataset page credits Kermani & Esmaeili (v3). This must be checked and almost certainly corrected before submission. The 68-vs-67 label-file discrepancy is itself worth a line in the data section and an integrity test.

findings.title: Kaggle derivative: 'PPG signal with Blood sugar level data' (muhammadyasirsaleem) containing clean-dataset.csv (46.76 MB) and notebook 'Predict Blood Glucose Level Using PPG Signals'
findings.source: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/muhammadyasirsaleem/ppg-signal-with-blood-sugar-level-data ; https://www.kaggle.com/code/muhammadyasirsaleem/predict-blood-glucose-level-using-ppg-signals ; a second Kaggle mirror of the raw set: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mhamza1018/ppg-glucose-dataset
findings.summary: Search confirms the Kaggle dataset ships a file named clean-dataset.csv (46.76 MB) and a companion notebook that regresses glucose on it. No published critique, discussion thread, or provenance statement about the file's label handling was found; the Kaggle page itself could not be fetched (403/bot check), so row count (844,946), upload date and download counts are unverified.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Supports the draft's statement that the derivative is 'widely circulated', but we found no prior public identification of the label-cycling artefact, which makes our characterisation novel. The claim 'the same column layout appears in other published pipelines' remains unsupported by anything found; soften or document it.

findings.title: The need to approximate the use-case in clinical machine learning (Saeb, Lonini, Jayaraman, Mohr, Kording)
findings.source: GigaScience 6(5):1-9, 2017, DOI 10.1093/gigascience/gix019 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5441397/); preprint bioRxiv 10.1101/059774 ('Voodoo Machine Learning for Clinical Predictions')
findings.summary: On the UCI smartphone HAR dataset (30 subjects, random forest), record-wise CV error stayed ~2% regardless of fold/subject count while subject-wise error was 27% (2 subjects) falling to ~7-9% (30 subjects); record-wise CV substantially underestimates true error on held-out data, subject-wise tracks it. Simulation: gap grows with between-subject variability and shrinks with more subjects. Literature survey: 28/62 clinical ML papers used record-wise CV; median reported error 5.6% (record-wise) vs 13.0% (subject-wise), P<0.01. Recommends subject-wise CV for diagnosis with global models, time-based splits for personal/prognostic models, tuning on training-only validation subsets.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Foundational citation for both our protocols (subject-wise for Mendeley, time-based for BIG IDEAs); the draft's Related Work currently cites nothing for 'subject-wise CV is the accepted remedy'.

findings.title: Using and understanding cross-validation strategies. Perspectives on Saeb et al. (Little, Varoquaux, Saeb, Lonini, Jayaraman, Mohr, Kording)
findings.summary: Three-part commentary: Little argues the key issue is dependence between records of the same subject; Varoquaux gives a confounding-structure formalism for why CV must mirror the deployment question; Saeb et al. respond. Establishes that the choice of CV unit must match the scientific claim (new subjects vs new time points).
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Supports stating explicitly which question each of our two protocols answers (new person vs future of the same person) and why the null model differs between them.

findings.title: Detecting the impact of subject characteristics on machine learning-based diagnostic applications (Chaibub Neto et al.)
findings.source: npj Digital Medicine 2:99, 2019, DOI 10.1038/s41746-019-0178-x (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6789029); preprint arXiv:1712.03120
findings.summary: Defines 'identity confounding' (record-wise splits let a classifier learn who the subject is) and gives a permutation test that shuffles labels at the subject level to quantify how much of a record-wise score is identity confounding; applied to several real datasets; recommends avoiding record-wise splits.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Provides a named concept and a statistical test we could add (subject-level label permutation) to show that any residual cross-subject r is not identity leakage; also relevant terminology for the Related Work.

findings.title: Data leakage in deep learning studies of translational EEG (Brookshire et al.)
findings.summary: Survey of 63 DNN-EEG studies: only 17 (27%) unambiguously avoided subject-level leakage; ~39 used segment-based splits. Reproductions: Alzheimer's classification accuracy 99.8% (segment split) vs 53.0% (subject split, CI includes chance); seizure detection 79.1% vs 65.1%. Recommends all segments of a subject in one partition, test set untouched by model selection, and expecting bias size to depend on sample size and model capacity.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Largest quantified inflation example (47 accuracy points) in a biosignal domain; cite in the 'leakage ladder' paragraph and to justify our fixed-budget/no-early-stopping rule.

findings.title: The NERVE-ML checklist: ensuring machine learning advances neural engineering (Carlson, Chavarriaga, Liu, Lotte, Lu)
findings.summary: Checklist plus four case studies showing validation choice changes conclusions. Mouse LFP (26 subjects): genotype AUC 0.980 (instance 5-fold) vs 0.639 (subject 5-fold); random-label AUC 0.979 under instance split (model memorises subjects). SEED-V EEG emotion (16 subjects): 1.000 instance-split accuracy vs 0.318 subject-group K-fold; random labels reach 0.937 under session grouping and only 0.209 (chance 0.20) under subject grouping. Sleep staging (20 subjects): 0.891 vs 0.827; subject-permuted labels still 0.588 under instance split. Autism EEG (293 subjects): >0.9 instance-level vs 0.72 subject-level. Guidance: split by subject when claims concern new subjects; match split to claim (instance/session/subject/time); report chance level and structure-preserving permutation tests; CV folds are dependent so use corrected tests (corrected resampled t-test); state scale of generalisation.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Closest thing to a domain checklist for IEEE-style biosignal ML papers; its 'random-label under leaky split' control is a cheap, powerful addition to our artefact section (train on the derivative CSV with shuffled subject labels). Its case tables are additional rungs for a leakage ladder.

findings.title: Investigation of Data Leakage in Deep-Learning-Based Blood Pressure Estimation Using Photoplethysmogram/Electrocardiogram (Yoshizawa, Yamamoto, Ohtsuki)
findings.summary: On the public cuff-less BP dataset, segment-level and record-level splits 'erroneously improved' mean-BP estimation relative to a (quasi-)subject-level split by Pearson r of 0.56 and 0.40 (PPG) and 0.82 and 0.69 (ECG); notes that a 'record' in that dataset is not a subject, a confusion repeated across prior studies; states most prior PPG/ECG-BP deep-learning studies incur leakage. (Numbers from abstract; full text behind IEEE paywall.)
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: An IEEE-journal precedent for a paper whose contribution is a leakage audit of a public PPG dataset, i.e. exactly our genre; the record-vs-subject confusion parallels Zeynali's '67 testing subjects'. Cite in Related Work and when motivating recording-level aggregation.

findings.title: Examining the challenges of blood pressure estimation via photoplethysmogram (Mehta, Kwatra, Jain, McDuff; Microsoft Research)
findings.source: Sci Rep 14:18318, 2024, DOI 10.1038/s41598-024-68862-1 (PMC11306225); preprint 'Can't Take the Pressure?' arXiv:2304.14916
findings.summary: Reviews 22 PPG-BP studies and finds 'a significant portion' have one or more of four pitfalls: data leakage (same patient or same windows in train/test), over-constrained label range, calibration not tested over time, aggressive signal filtering (by their Table 1 roughly 16/22 have split problems). Quantified ladder on PPG2ABP: SD 23.1 mmHg (no overlap) -> 16.2 (domain overlap) -> 8.01 (data overlap). Restricting SBP range 65-200 -> 75-150 improves SD 15.8 -> 12.4. A 'naive calibration' that predicts a constant per record (SD 8.61) beats their calibrated network (9.82) and uncalibrated (10.9), which they call a flaw in evaluation practice. Raising a signal-quality threshold to 0.8 improved performance 29.7% but discarded 63% of data.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Direct analogue in the sister PPG task: constant-per-subject predictor beating the network is exactly our BIG IDEAs finding; label-range restriction is the analogue of euglycaemic cohorts making Clarke zone A trivial. Strong citation for our 'reporting recommendations'.

findings.title: Subject Cross Validation in Human Activity Recognition (Dehghani, Glatard, Shihab)
findings.summary: k-fold CV 'artificially increases the performance of recognizers by about 10%', rising to 16% when overlapping sliding windows are used; overlapping windows gave no real gain; recommends subject CV.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Quantifies the separate contribution of window overlap to leakage; relevant because our Mendeley pipeline uses 50%-overlap windows within a recording, which is harmless only because we split by subject and aggregate per recording - worth stating.

findings.title: Too Good To Be True: performance overestimation in (re)current practices for Human Activity Recognition (Tello, Degeler, Lazovik)
findings.summary: Random k-fold vs group-based splits: MILAN RF weighted F1 95.17 -> 56.64; PAMAP2 GNN F1 91.97 -> 85.73; MHEALTH GNN F1 97.95 -> 85.77 (paper states range 5.4-33.6 points). Mechanism: sliding windows with step << window length put near-duplicate neighbours of each test window in training.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Another rung for the ladder, and the clearest statement of the window-neighbour mechanism that also motivates our 1-h guard gap on BIG IDEAs.

findings.title: Model Evaluation Approaches for Human Activity Recognition from Time-Series Data (Hinkle & Metsis, Texas State)
findings.summary: 1D-CNN on MobiAct: stratified (subject-mixed) split accuracy 99.3% vs subject-attribute split 96.9% (error 0.7% vs 3.1%); UniMiB SHAR 93.9% vs 92.3%. Also cites an RNN study dropping from 88.4% (5-fold) to 73.2% (LOSO). Shows large per-subject variance under LOSO.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Minor rung; useful mainly to show that error, not accuracy, is the right scale (4x error inflation hidden in a 2.4-point accuracy change) - the same argument as our MAE-vs-zone-A point.

findings.title: Let's (not) stick together: pairwise similarity biases cross-validation in activity recognition (Hammerla & Ploetz)
findings.summary: Shows random CV is biased for segmented time series because adjacent segments are statistically dependent, and that common evaluation does not test generalisation to new users; proposes meta-segmented CV. (Full text not retrieved; numbers not verified.)
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Canonical early citation for temporal-dependence leakage; cite alongside Saeb.

findings.title: Empirical investigation of multi-source cross-validation in clinical ECG classification (Leinonen, Wong, Vasankari, Wahab, Nadarajah, Kaisti, Airola)
findings.summary: Standard K-fold CV 'systemically overestimates' performance when the claim is generalisation to new data sources; leave-source-out CV has near-zero bias but higher variance.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Supports the top rung of the ladder (new site/device) and our use of two independent sources (finger pulse sensor vs wrist E4) as a form of cross-source evidence.

findings.title: Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science (Kapoor & Narayanan)
findings.summary: Taxonomy of eight leakage types: L1.1 no test set; L1.2 pre-processing across splits; L1.3 feature selection across splits; L1.4 duplicates; L2 illegitimate features (proxies for the outcome); L3.1 temporal leakage; L3.2 non-independence between train and test (e.g. same patients); L3.3 sampling bias. Leakage found in 22 reviews across 17 fields affecting at least 294 papers; after correction ML no longer beat logistic regression in the civil-war case study (Wang AUC gap 0.14 -> 0.01). Proposes 21-question 'model info sheets' to attest clean train-test separation, feature legitimacy and test-set relevance.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Gives us a vocabulary: our label-replication artefact is a label-construction leak that is not in the eight types (closest are L1.2 and L2), which is a genuine contribution to name; identity leakage is L3.2; early stopping on the held-out subject is L1.x. A filled model info sheet as supplementary material would be a credible reviewer-facing artefact.

findings.title: Common pitfalls and recommendations for using machine learning to detect and prognosticate for COVID-19 using chest radiographs and CT scans (Roberts et al.)
findings.summary: Of 62 studies passing quality screening, none was judged of potential clinical use; 45/62 high and 11/62 unclear risk of bias in participants; recommendations in five areas (data, evaluation, reproducibility, manuscript documentation, peer review).
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: Standard citation that negative-result / audit papers of ML evaluation are publishable at top venues; also used CLAIM/PROBAST-style assessment, which reviewers may ask us to self-apply.

findings.title: Cross-validation failure: small sample sizes lead to large error bars (Varoquaux)
findings.summary: CV accuracy estimates carry roughly +/-10% uncertainty at n~100; the standard error across folds strongly underestimates true uncertainty; repeated random splits preferred over LOO but do not fix the width.
findings.relevance_to_our_paper: With 23 subjects / 67 recordings our confidence intervals are wide; we should report bootstrap CIs on recording-level MAE and r and avoid fold-SE error bars, and we can use this to explain why a single 4-subject test set (as in Syamsul & Kim, and our withdrawn draft) is uninformative.

findings.title: Widespread use of invalid statistical tests in biomedical machine learning (Zeng, Li, Zhang, Tan et al., University of Melbourne)
